from pysat.solvers import Glucose3
from itertools import combinations

n = 14
# Variables: x_{i,j} for 0 <= i < j < 14
# Map (i,j) to variable index
def var(i, j):
    if i > j:
        i, j = j, i
    return i * n + j + 1  # 1-indexed for SAT

solver = Glucose3()

# Fixed edges
solver.add_clause([var(9, 13)])
solver.add_clause([var(4, 13)])

# No 3-cycles
for i, j, k in combinations(range(n), 3):
    # Forbid x_{i,j} AND x_{j,k} AND x_{k,i}
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, j), -var(j, k), -var(k, i)])

# No 4-cycles
for i, j, k, l in combinations(range(n), 4):
    # A 4-cycle on {i,j,k,l} can be (i,j,k,l), (i,j,l,k), or (i,k,j,l)
    # We need to forbid all three
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, j), -var(j, k), -var(k, l), -var(l, i)])
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, j), -var(j, l), -var(l, k), -var(k, i)])
    solver.add_clause([-var(i, k), -var(k, j), -var(j, l), -var(l, i)])

# No 5-cycles
for i, j, k, l, m in combinations(range(n), 5):
    # A 5-cycle on {i,j,k,l,m} has (5-1)!/2 = 12 distinct orderings
    # We need to forbid all of them
    from itertools import permutations
    vertices = [i, j, k, l, m]
    seen = set()
    for perm in permutations(vertices):
        # Normalize: start with smallest, go in direction of smaller second element
        cycle = list(perm)
        min_idx = cycle.index(min(cycle))
        cycle = cycle[min_idx:] + cycle[:min_idx]
        if cycle[1] > cycle[-1]:
            cycle = [cycle[0]] + cycle[1:][::-1]
        key = tuple(cycle)
        if key in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(key)
        clause = [-var(cycle[t], cycle[(t+1)%5]) for t in range(5)]
        solver.add_clause(clause)

print("Solving...")
if solver.solve():
    model = solver.get_model()
    edges = []
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i+1, n):
            v = var(i, j)
            if v in model:
                edges.append((i, j))

    adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]

        adj[v].append(u)

                    parent[v] = u
                    queue.append(v)
